title: Evidence for Three-component Interlayer Coherent Exciton Condensation
authors: Subi Du, Xiaohan Zhang, Hongxi Song, Siyu Fan, Yiduo Wang, Zhenyu Wang, Song Liu, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Jiangping Hu, Yang Xu
abstract: Increasing the number of internal components in a quantum many-body system can host collective orders inaccessible to simpler settings. Quantum Hall bilayers provide a canonical realization of interlayer exciton condensation, yet extending such coherence across three independently addressable electronic fluids has remained elusive. Here we report evidence for three-component interlayer coherent exciton condensation in triple-layer graphene system. Using Rydberg excitons in an adjacent WSe2 monolayer as a layer-sensitive optical probe, we resolve interaction-induced incompressibility at zeroth-Landau-level crossings for all three pairwise layer combinations, establishing top-middle, middle-bottom and top-bottom exciton condensate channels within the same device. Independent control of displacement field and interlayer bias continuously tunes these pairwise states towards a regime where Landau levels from all three layers approach simultaneous degeneracy. At their convergence, incompressibility persists while the exciton energy and spectral weight evolve smoothly between the pairwise limits, suggesting coherent participation of all three layers in a single three-component state. More broadly, the ability to independently control layer potentials and engineer interlayer interactions establishes multilayer graphene as a programmable synthetic dimension for exploring higher-component quantum Hall order and simulating strongly correlated quantum matter.
summary: This work reports experimental evidence for three-component interlayer coherent exciton condensation in a triple-layer graphene system using a WSe2 optical probe. By independently controlling layer potentials, the researchers demonstrated a continuous transition from pairwise to a three-component correlated state. This establishes multilayer graphene as a programmable platform for exploring higher-order quantum Hall physics.
main_problem: The research investigates the existence and characteristics of three-component interlayer coherent exciton condensation in a triple-layer graphene system, extending beyond previously studied bilayer systems.
main_result: The authors report evidence for a continuous transition from pairwise to a three-component coherent state, marked by persistent incompressibility when all three layer-derived Landau levels approach simultaneous degeneracy.
method: The study uses layer-sensitive optical spectroscopy employing Rydberg excitons in an adjacent WSe2 monolayer as a probe to map out the system's phase diagram.
model_or_system: The physical system is a triple-layer graphene (TLG) heterostructure, whose electronic structure is analyzed using coupled electrostatic charge-balance equations. The coherence is studied in the context of Quantum Hall physics.
key_observables: Optical signature of QH incompressibility, layer-resolved ZLL crossings, and the evolution of exciton energy/spectral weight across different coherence regimes.
important_parameters:
Interlayer bias voltage, displacement field, and the total filling factor ($
u_{tot}$), which are tuned to control the system's electronic state.
main_assumptions: The WSe2 optical response provides intrinsic layer sensitivity, and the analysis relies on solving coupled electrostatic equations derived from capacitance networks.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device structure, layer-resolved ZLL crossings in double and triple layers, and phase diagrams showing the continuous tuning from pairwise to three-component coherent states.
paper_structure: The paper builds from establishing two-component coherence in double-layer graphene, then extends the analysis to triple-layer graphene, mapping out the phase space by tuning external fields to observe the transition into the three-component coherent regime.
why_interesting: The ability to engineer and observe higher-component quantum Hall order in a tunable solid-state platform like multilayer graphene provides a clean, controllable model for studying complex many-body correlations.
